weeks.title: Grace: A Free Gift
weeks.theme: Salvation isn’t earned by works; it is by grace through faith—God’s free gift.
group: What did you used to think “getting into heaven” depended on?
Why is receiving a free gift actually hard for people?
Which prayer is more like yours—the Pharisee’s or the tax collector’s?
weeks.guide: Many Chinese seekers are deeply shaped by the idea of “doing good and accumulating merit.” Grace may feel foreign, even “too cheap.” This week, use images like “a gift” or “someone paying for you,” and explain that grace isn’t cheap—Jesus paid the price—and that grace isn’t a license to do as we please but power to change. Watch for whether they hold back because they feel unworthy, and gently tell them: it is grace precisely because we are unworthy.
weeks.meet: This week, share with the person walking with you: have you ever received a gift that made you feel “I don’t deserve this”? How did you respond?
weeks.keyText: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.

lessons.title: By Grace, Through Faith
text: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God,
not of works, that no one would boast.
lessons.hear:
Imagine on your birthday a friend hands you a beautiful gift, and you pull out your wallet: “How much? Let me pay you.” Your friend would be hurt. A gift is a gift precisely because it is free; once you pay, it becomes a transaction.

The Bible says: “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast” (Ephesians 2:8-9). “Grace” is love we don’t deserve yet receive. Salvation is God’s gift, not something we buy with good behavior. Why does God arrange it this way? “That no one would boast.” If salvation depended on works, good people would become proud and bad people would despair; but grace puts everyone in the same place: all need it, and all can receive it.

What does “through faith” mean? Faith is like reaching out your hand to take a gift. The hand earns nothing; it only receives. You don’t have to become a good person first or practice religion for years. You only need to admit that you need it, believe that what God offers is real, and reach out to take it. It is the simplest thing in the world—and the hardest: simple because there is nothing to do, hard because we must lay down our pride.
lessons.light: Wanting to be saved by our own works is another form of the self-centered life: I want to do it myself. Receiving grace requires humbly admitting, “I can’t; I need you.” Humility overcomes pride, beginning with receiving grace.
think: What did you used to think salvation depended on?
“Once you pay, a gift becomes a transaction.” What does this picture bring to mind?
What in your heart resists receiving free grace?
lessons.speak: God, I always thought I had to be good enough for you to accept me. So salvation is a gift you give freely. I want to lay down my own efforts and pride and reach out to receive your grace. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Give someone a small gift today (a coffee, a blessing) with no expectation of return, and notice what “giving freely” feels like.
lessons.quick: A gift can’t be bought; salvation can’t be earned.

lessons.title: Not by Our Own Righteousness
text: But when the kindness of God our Savior and his love toward mankind appeared,
not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit,
lessons.hear:
In Chinese culture we grow up hearing “good deeds are rewarded, bad deeds are punished,” and we often hear about “accumulating merit.” These ideas encourage people to do good and have value. But if we use them to handle our relationship with God, we hit a big problem: can our good deeds cancel out our sins?

Imagine someone who ran a red light and injured a person. In court he says, “Your Honor, I usually do lots of good deeds and give lots of money.” The judge would say, “Your good deeds are commendable, but they don’t cancel the law you broke today.” The Bible says: “not by works of righteousness which we did ourselves, but according to his mercy, he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewing by the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5).

We are saved not because we are good enough but because God is merciful. That doesn’t mean good works don’t matter; it means good works aren’t the cause of salvation but the result. An apple tree bears apples not to become an apple tree, but because it already is one. God first gives us new life, and good works grow naturally out of that new life.
lessons.light: Life first, then living. We don’t gain life by good behavior; we bear good behavior once we have new life. Reverse the order and faith becomes a burden; get the order right and faith becomes joy.
think: What sayings about “accumulating merit” or “good deeds bring good rewards” did you grow up with?
What does the courtroom picture help you understand?
How do you understand “good works are the result of salvation, not the cause”?
lessons.speak: God, I once thought good behavior could earn your acceptance. Thank you for showing me that I am saved because of your mercy, not my own righteousness. Please give me new life, and let good works grow naturally from within. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Think: is there a “good deed” you did mainly to feel better than others? Confess it to God and thank him for his mercy.
lessons.quick: Good works aren’t the cause of salvation but the fruit of new life.

lessons.title: The Prodigal Comes to Himself
text: But when he came to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger!
I will get up and go to my father, and will tell him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight.
I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants.”’
“He arose and came to his father. But while he was still far off, his father saw him and was moved with compassion, and ran, fell on his neck, and kissed him.
lessons.hear:
Let’s return to the prodigal son. When he had spent everything and was faint with hunger in the pigpen, the Bible says, “he came to himself” (Luke 15:17)—as if he finally woke up and saw his real self and his real situation: “How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough to spare, and I’m dying with hunger!”

He decided to go home and even prepared a confession: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and in your sight. I am no more worthy to be called your son. Make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:18-19). He planned to come home as a hired worker and repay with his labor. But he never imagined that his father wouldn’t even let him finish the “make me a hired servant” part. The father gave him a robe, a ring and sandals, restoring his place as a son.

That is the astonishing thing about grace: we think, “Let me do something to make up for it”; God thinks, “Welcome home—you are my child.” The prodigal’s waking up and turning around were necessary, but his identity wasn’t won back by performance—the father restored it freely. Maybe you are waking up in a pigpen too. Then get up. The road home is always open.
lessons.light: Coming to ourselves means returning to our place: seeing clearly who we are and who the Father is. Pride would rather starve in the pigpen than go home; humility gets up and walks toward the Father. That step home is a step of humility.
think: When the prodigal “came to himself,” what did he see?
He planned to be a hired servant, but the father restored him as a son. What’s the difference?
Is there an area of your life where you need to “come to yourself”?
lessons.speak: Father, I too have left home and looked for satisfaction elsewhere, only to become emptier. Today I am waking up, and I want to get up and come home. Thank you that you don’t want me as a hired servant, but as your child. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write: “If I came back to the Father now, I would want to tell him…” Write three sentences in your own words.
lessons.quick: We want to repay as servants; the Father welcomes us home as children.

lessons.title: Not Working, but Believing
text: Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed.
But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness.
lessons.hear:
At work we all know the rule: you get paid for what you do. That’s a wage—it’s owed. Paul uses this idea: “Now to him who works, the reward is not counted as grace, but as something owed. But to him who doesn’t work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is accounted for righteousness” (Romans 4:4-5).

“Justifies” is a legal term meaning “declares not guilty.” God doesn’t declare good people righteous; he declares the “ungodly” righteous! How can that be? Because Jesus has already borne the punishment for us. It’s like a bill full of debt being exchanged for one stamped “Paid”—and even more wonderful, Jesus’ perfection is credited to our account. This is called justification by faith.

For someone who has always tried hard to be “good enough,” this is a great release. You no longer have to carry the burden of “I haven’t done enough,” or fear that God will reject you because you performed badly today. Your identity rests on Jesus’ work, not on your performance. This isn’t an invitation to laziness; it’s an invitation to begin again in rest.
lessons.light: Let God be God: only God can justify the ungodly. Let people be people: all we can do is reach out and believe. When we stop proving ourselves by performance, we are released from comparison, anxiety and pride—the freedom grace brings.
think: Where in your life do you constantly feel “I haven’t done enough”?
Does “God justifies the ungodly” surprise you? Why?
If your identity didn’t depend on performance, how would your life be different?
lessons.speak: God who justifies the ungodly, I keep trying to prove myself by performance, and I’m so tired. Thank you that I don’t have to work to earn your acceptance. I choose to trust you and believe that Jesus has paid for everything. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Whenever you do something today, remind yourself: “I’m not doing this to be loved; I’m doing it because I am loved.”
lessons.quick: God justifies the ungodly—by Jesus, not by my performance.

lessons.title: Two Men Praying
text: “Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.
The Pharisee stood and prayed by himself like this: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector.
I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.’
But the tax collector, standing far away, wouldn’t even lift up his eyes to heaven, but beat his chest, saying, ‘God, be merciful to me, a sinner!’
I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”
lessons.hear:
Jesus told a story: “Two men went up into the temple to pray; one was a Pharisee, and the other was a tax collector.” The Pharisee was the model religious person of his day; the tax collector was a notorious sinner and traitor. The Pharisee prayed: “God, I thank you that I am not like the rest of men: extortionists, unrighteous, adulterers, or even like this tax collector. I fast twice a week. I give tithes of all that I get.”

But the tax collector stood far off, wouldn’t even lift his eyes to heaven, and beat his chest, saying: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13). Jesus said, “I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 18:14).

This story shocked its hearers. The Pharisee’s problem wasn’t his good behavior but that he relied on it and looked down on others. The tax collector had no good works to offer—only a broken, humble heart. God doesn’t look at our résumé; he looks at the heart. This week we saw that grace is free. Next week we’ll look at what it means to truly receive this grace.
lessons.light: Humility is the key to revival: God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble. The Pharisee left his place and sat in the judge’s seat; the tax collector returned to his place and admitted he was a sinner. The focus isn’t others but myself.
think: Are you more like the Pharisee or the tax collector? Think honestly.
How many times does the Pharisee say “I”?
Are you willing to pray, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner”?
lessons.speak: God, be merciful to me, a sinner! I no longer want to stand before you on my own good behavior, or look down on others. I come to you with nothing but a heart that needs you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Today, whenever you feel like criticizing someone, pause and pray in your heart: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
lessons.quick: God doesn’t read our résumé—he looks for a humble heart.

weeks.title: Repent and Believe: Turning Home
weeks.theme: Repentance is turning away from the self-centered path; faith is entrusting your life to Jesus.
group: What did you used to think “repentance” meant?
What is the difference between believing in Jesus and “knowing about” Jesus?
Jesus is knocking at the door. What state is the door of your heart in right now?
weeks.guide: This week, help the seeker understand that repentance isn’t just feeling sorry but a change of direction, and faith isn’t just mental agreement but entrusting one’s life. The chair illustration helps: knowing a chair will hold you is different from actually sitting down. Watch whether they are ready to receive Jesus. If they say they are, you don’t need to wait for week 11—lead them in the prayer of commitment (see “Prayer of Commitment” on the Journey tab) and record their spiritual birthday.
weeks.meet: This week, read Revelation 3:20 with the person walking with you, and quietly ask yourself: am I willing to open the door to Jesus?
weeks.keyText: and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and God’s Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News.”

lessons.title: Turning Around
text: Now after John was taken into custody, Jesus came into Galilee, preaching the Good News of God’s Kingdom,
and saying, “The time is fulfilled, and God’s Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News.”
lessons.hear:
The first words of Jesus’ public preaching were: “The time is fulfilled, and God’s Kingdom is at hand! Repent, and believe in the Good News” (Mark 1:15). There are two actions here: repent and believe. They are like two sides of one coin—one side turning away, the other turning toward.

The word “repent” originally means “to change one’s mind,” and by extension, “to turn around.” Imagine someone driving south who realizes his destination is north. No matter how sorry he feels or how much he cries, if he keeps driving south he only gets farther away. Repentance isn’t just feeling bad; it is turning around. Biblical repentance is turning from the self-centered road toward God.

Repentance doesn’t require you to become perfect overnight; it is a change of direction. If the direction is right, going slowly is fine; if the direction is wrong, the faster you go, the more dangerous it is. Jesus said “God’s Kingdom is at hand,” meaning the good news of God reigning has come right to you—now is the time to turn.
lessons.light: Repentance is turning from “I reign” to “let Jesus reign.” This is the most important change of direction in life: from the self-centered old life to the selfless new life. The first step in changing our mindset is a change of direction.
think: Is “repentance is turning around, not just feeling sorry” the same as your previous understanding?
What is your life currently centered on?
If you turned around, what would you most need to turn away from?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you said, “Repent, and believe in the Good News.” Now I understand that repentance is turning around. I am willing to turn from the self-centered road toward you. Please give me strength. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Draw a line on the ground (or imagine one). Stand on one side and name what you want to turn away from, then turn around, step across, and say: “Lord, I turn to you.”
lessons.quick: Repentance isn’t only sorrow—it’s turning around.

lessons.title: Believing Is Trusting
text: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.
For God didn’t send his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world should be saved through him.
He who believes in him is not judged. He who doesn’t believe has been judged already, because he has not believed in the name of the only born Son of God.
lessons.hear:
John 3:16 has been called “the gospel in a nutshell”: “For God so loved the world, that he gave his only born Son, that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal life.” This verse contains God’s love, God’s gift, our response and two possible outcomes. What is our response? To “believe in him.”

But what does “believe” mean? A tightrope walker once pushed a wheelbarrow back and forth over a waterfall. He asked the crowd, “Do you believe I can push a person across?” Everyone shouted, “Yes!” He said, “Then who will get into the wheelbarrow?” Suddenly no one spoke. Many people “believe” in Jesus the way that crowd believed; the Bible means the kind of belief that gets into the wheelbarrow.

Faith isn’t only agreeing in your head that “Jesus is the Son of God”; it is putting your life in his hands, trusting and relying on him—like sitting in a chair: knowing it will hold you is different from putting your whole weight on it. Jesus says, “He who believes in him is not judged” (John 3:18). Those who believe no longer live under condemnation and fear.
lessons.light: Faith is humble entrusting: admitting I can’t, believing he can. The self-centered person trusts only himself; the selfless person entrusts himself to Jesus. The moment you get into the wheelbarrow is the beginning of letting Jesus be Lord.
think: In the tightrope story, are you like the shouting crowd or the one who gets in?
What does the difference between “knowing the chair is sturdy” and “sitting down” make you think of?
What worries you most about entrusting your life to Jesus?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I don’t want only to know about you; I want to trust you. I put my life, my worries and my future into your hands. Help me truly trust you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: When you sit down on a chair today, ask: have I put my whole weight on Jesus? Hand one worry to him.
lessons.quick: Faith isn’t shouting “I believe”—it’s getting into the wheelbarrow.

lessons.title: Born Anew
text: Jesus answered him, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom.”
Nicodemus said to him, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”
Jesus answered, “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born of water and Spirit, he can’t enter into God’s Kingdom.
That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit.
Don’t marvel that I said to you, ‘You must all be born anew.’
lessons.hear:
A prominent Jewish teacher named Nicodemus came to Jesus secretly at night. He was learned, moral and sincere. Yet Jesus told him: “Most certainly I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom” (John 3:3). Nicodemus was puzzled: “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother’s womb and be born?”

The new birth Jesus spoke of isn’t a second physical birth, but being “born of the Spirit”—born from above, the birth of spiritual life. He said: “That which is born of the flesh is flesh. That which is born of the Spirit is spirit” (John 3:6). Nicodemus didn’t need more religious knowledge or better character; he needed an entirely new life.

The same is true for every one of us. Religion can decorate a person, but it can’t give new life. Dress a caterpillar in beautiful clothes and it is still a caterpillar; it needs a transformation into a butterfly. When a person repents and trusts Jesus, the Holy Spirit brings new life inside—this is being born again. It isn’t our effort; it is God’s work. What we can do is come to Jesus with our questions, as Nicodemus did.
lessons.light: New birth is a change of life, not religious decoration. The old self-centered life can’t be patched up; only life from above can make us selfless. Life first: all real change begins with new life.
think: Nicodemus was very moral. Why did Jesus say he still needed to be born anew?
What does the difference between a dressed-up caterpillar and a butterfly bring to mind?
Do you think what you need is “decoration” or “new birth”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, like Nicodemus I come to you with many questions. Now I see that I don’t just need to be a little better—I need a brand-new life. Please give me new birth. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Find a picture of a butterfly (or choose one in the app’s card studio) and make a card with “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
lessons.quick: Religion can decorate us; only new birth renews us.

lessons.title: Times of Refreshing
text: “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord,
lessons.hear:
Peter was preaching to a large crowd at the temple. They had just seen a man lame from birth healed in Jesus’ name. Peter told them: you rejected Jesus and killed him, but God raised him from the dead. Then he said: “Repent therefore, and turn again, that your sins may be blotted out, so that there may come times of refreshing from the presence of the Lord” (Acts 3:19).

“Blotted out” referred to wiping writing off parchment or a wax tablet. Ancient ink contained no acid and could be wiped clean with a damp cloth, as if nothing had ever been written. God says that those who repent and turn again have their sins wiped away like that—not recorded for a later reckoning, but blotted out.

“Times of refreshing” carries the sense of cool air, a chance to catch your breath—like walking a long way in the heat and finally stepping into cool shade. Many people carry the weight of guilt for years: a word spoken wrongly, a wrong thing done, a past that hurt others. God invites you: repent and turn again, let him blot out your sins, and let your heart breathe.
lessons.light: Guilt is a heavy burden; people often try to make up for it themselves and only grow more tired. Repenting and turning again means laying the burden down before God. Only the forgiven can truly walk forward lightly.
think: Have you carried guilt in your heart for a long time?
How does the image of “blotting out” make you feel?
Where do you most need “times of refreshing”?
lessons.speak: God, I have been carrying some heavy things for a long time—things I did wrong. I am willing to repent and turn again. Please blot out my sins and let my heart be refreshed. Thank you for your forgiveness. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: In pencil, write one thing you feel guilty about. Confess it to God, then erase it with an eraser.
lessons.quick: God doesn’t record my sins—he blots them out.

lessons.title: Jesus Knocks at the Door
text: Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me.
lessons.hear:
A famous painting shows Jesus holding a lamp, standing outside an ivy-covered door and knocking. Someone pointed out what seemed like the painter’s mistake: there is no handle on the door. The painter answered, “That’s no mistake. This door can only be opened from the inside.”

Jesus says: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, then I will come in to him and will dine with him, and he with me” (Revelation 3:20). Jesus doesn’t break in; he respects your choice. He stands outside, knocking gently and patiently. He knocks in many ways: a verse that moves you, a friend who cares, a crisis in life, an inexpressible longing in your heart.

“Dine with him” is a very intimate picture—like friends sharing a meal and talking. Jesus doesn’t want a distant worshiper; he wants a close relationship. This week we have seen that repentance is turning and faith is trusting. Next week we talk about the most important decision: opening the door and receiving Jesus into your life. If you want to open the door today, you don’t have to wait until next week.
lessons.light: The handle is on the inside because God respects human choice. Opening the door means letting Jesus change from a guest outside to the master of the house—letting Jesus reign. This is the most important decision of a person’s life.
think: What does “this door can only be opened from the inside” mean to you?
Have you sensed Jesus knocking in your life recently?
If you open the door, what would you most hope Jesus would do in your life?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I hear you knocking. Thank you for waiting for me so patiently. I want to open the door and let you come into my life and dine with me. Please prepare my heart. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: When you walk through your front door today, pause and ask: is the door of my heart open to Jesus? If you are ready, go to “Prayer of Commitment” on the Journey tab, or pray with the person walking with you.
lessons.quick: Jesus is knocking—the handle is on my side.

weeks.title: Receiving Jesus as Lord of My Life
weeks.theme: All who receive Jesus and believe in his name are given the right to become children of God.
group: What does “receiving Jesus” mean to you?
Confessing with the mouth, believing in the heart—which feels harder?
Are you ready to receive Jesus? If not, what is holding you back?
weeks.guide: This is commitment week. Please arrange a face-to-face (or video) meeting and gently ask: “Would you like to receive Jesus as your Savior and Lord?” If they are willing, lead them line by line in the prayer of commitment (there is a model on the Journey tab), then help them record their spiritual birthday, bless them, and tell them: this is a beginning, not the end. If they aren’t ready, don’t pressure them—ask about their concerns and keep walking with them. The first four weeks after commitment matter most; stay in close contact.
weeks.meet: This week, set a time to meet with the person walking with you. If you are ready, you can pray the prayer of commitment together; if not, share your concerns honestly.
weeks.keyText: But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name:

lessons.title: Receive Him
text: He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him.
But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name:
who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
lessons.hear:
John writes a heartbreaking line: “He came to his own, and those who were his own didn’t receive him” (John 1:11). The Lord who made the world came into the world, and the world didn’t recognize him; he came to his own people, and they rejected him. But John continues: “But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12).

“Receive” is an everyday word, like welcoming a guest into your home. But receiving Jesus isn’t just letting him be a guest; it’s letting him be the master of the house. Imagine your life as a house with a living room, a study, a bedroom, a kitchen—and a storage room you don’t want anyone to see. Receiving Jesus means handing him the whole ring of keys and letting him into every room.

And the result? “To become God’s children.” Not by bloodline, human will or effort, but “born… of God” (John 1:13). The moment someone receives Jesus, their identity changes: from God’s enemy to God’s child, from orphan to someone with a Father. It is the greatest change in a person’s life.
lessons.light: Receiving Jesus as master of the house means letting Jesus reign. No longer “my house, my rules,” but “Lord, this is your home.” Handing over the keys looks like loss, but it is gain: the identity of a child of God.
think: If your life were a house, which room would you least want Jesus to enter?
What is the difference between letting Jesus be a guest and letting him be the master?
What draws you to the identity of “a child of God”?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I want to receive you—not only as my guest but as my master. I hand you the keys of my life; every room is open to you. Thank you for giving me the right to become a child of God. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Draw a simple house with several rooms (work, family, money, relationships, leisure, the past). In each room write: “Lord, this is yours too.”
lessons.quick: Receiving Jesus means handing him the keys of my life.

lessons.title: Confess with Your Mouth, Believe in Your Heart
text: that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
For with the heart one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation.
lessons.hear:
The Bible states clearly how a person is saved: “that if you will confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes resulting in righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made resulting in salvation” (Romans 10:9-10).

There are two parts: believing in the heart and confessing with the mouth. Believing in the heart is inner trust: trusting that Jesus died for me and that God raised him from the dead. Confessing with the mouth is speaking that belief aloud: “Jesus is Lord.” In the early church, saying “Jesus is Lord” came at a cost, because the Roman Empire demanded people say “Caesar is lord.” Confessing Jesus as Lord declared: the highest authority over my life belongs to Jesus.

Why confess with the mouth? Think of a wedding: two people loving each other in their hearts isn’t enough; they also say “I do” in front of others. Saying it is confirmation and commitment. Today you can try saying this sentence aloud: “Jesus is Lord.” If you already believe in your heart, this sentence is your declaration of faith.
lessons.light: “Jesus is Lord” is the heart of 321: let Jesus reign. Confessing with the mouth declares to heaven and earth that my life is no longer run by me. It’s a simple sentence that changes a whole life.
think: Which feels easier to you—believing in the heart or confessing with the mouth?
What might saying “Jesus is Lord” cost you in your life?
Are you willing to say it aloud today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I believe in my heart that you died for me and that God raised you from the dead. Now I confess with my mouth: Jesus is Lord—Lord of my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Find a quiet place and say aloud three times: “Jesus is Lord—Lord of my life.” Then notice what changes in your heart.
lessons.quick: Believe in the heart, confess with the mouth: Jesus is Lord.

lessons.title: Let Him Be Lord
text: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?
Everyone who comes to me, and hears my words and does them, I will show you who he is like.

He is like a man building a house, who dug and went deep and laid a foundation on the rock. When a flood arose, the stream broke against that house, and could not shake it, because it was founded on the rock.
lessons.hear:
Jesus said something very direct: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and don’t do the things which I say?” (Luke 6:46). Calling him Lord but not listening is like an employee who greets the boss every day but never does what the boss asks.

Then Jesus told a parable. The one who hears his words and does them “is like a man building a house, who dug and went deep and laid a foundation on the rock. When a flood arose, the stream broke against that house, and could not shake it, because it was founded on the rock” (Luke 6:48). The one who hears and doesn’t do is like a house built on soil—when the flood comes, it collapses.

Receiving Jesus as Lord isn’t only a prayer; it is the start of a new way of living: from now on, asking his will in matters big and small. This isn’t pressure but protection. Life’s floods will come—illness, job loss, grief, conflict. Those whose foundation is on the rock may be battered, but they won’t fall. Letting Jesus be Lord means digging deep and setting your life on the rock.
lessons.light: Letting Jesus reign isn’t a slogan; it’s every choice in daily life. Hearing and doing is faith in practice—moving from “Conviction” to “Practice” in the eight steps of changing our mindset.
think: What “flood” are you most likely to face in life?
Have you ever called him Lord without doing what he says?
In what small matter this week can you let Jesus be Lord?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I don’t want only to call you “Lord, Lord”; I truly want you to be my Lord. Help me do what I hear, and build my life on you, the rock. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Before making a decision today (buying something, replying to a message, planning your time), ask in your heart: “Lord, what do you want?”
lessons.quick: Letting Jesus be Lord means building my life on the rock.

lessons.title: Whoever Calls on the Name of the Lord
text: For, “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
lessons.hear:
“For, ‘Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved’” (Romans 10:13). This is one of the widest invitations in the Bible. “Whoever”—no matter who you are, what you have done, how educated you are or where you come from. “Call on”—cry out to him, pray to him. “Will be saved”—not “might,” but “will.”

You don’t need a special place, ritual or language—only a sincere heart speaking to God. Below is a simple prayer. You can read it as it is, or say it in your own words. What matters isn’t the words but your heart:

“Dear Father, I admit that I am a sinner. I have often lived centered on myself and turned away from you. I believe that Jesus is the Son of God, that he died on the cross for my sins and rose from the dead on the third day. I now turn from my sin to you, and I receive Jesus as the Savior and Lord of my life. Please forgive my sins, give me new life, and let your Holy Spirit live in my heart. From today on, I want to let Jesus reign and follow him all my life.”
lessons.light: This moment is the starting point from the old self to the new: from a self-centered life to a Jesus-centered life. It doesn’t depend on my resolve but on God’s promise: “Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
think: What does the word “whoever” in “whoever calls on the name of the Lord” mean to you?
Reading the prayer, which line moves you most? Which still raises questions?
Are you willing to pray this prayer today?
lessons.speak: Dear Father, I admit that I am a sinner. I have often lived centered on myself and turned away from you. I believe that Jesus is the Son of God, that he died on the cross for my sins and rose from the dead on the third day. I now turn from my sin to you, and I receive Jesus as the Savior and Lord of my life. Please forgive my sins, give me new life, and let your Holy Spirit live in my heart. From today on, I want to let Jesus reign and follow him all my life. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: If you prayed this prayer today, go to the Journey tab, tap “I received Jesus,” record your spiritual birthday, and tell the person walking with you. If you’re not ready yet, write down what makes you hesitate.
lessons.quick: Whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

lessons.title: Joy in Heaven
text: I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance.
Even so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner repenting.”
lessons.hear:
Jesus told three stories of things lost and found: a lost sheep, a lost coin, a lost son. Each ends with celebration. The shepherd finds his sheep, carries it on his shoulders, and calls his friends to rejoice; the woman finds her coin and invites her neighbors to rejoice. Jesus said: “I tell you that even so there will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents, than over ninety-nine righteous people who need no repentance” (Luke 15:7).

Can you imagine? When one person turns back to God, heaven throws a party. Jesus also said: “Even so, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner repenting” (Luke 15:10). Your decision is no small thing; it makes heaven rejoice. God doesn’t accept you reluctantly—he welcomes you with joy.

If you have received Jesus this week, congratulations! Today is your spiritual birthday. You may feel overwhelmed, or you may feel nothing special—both are fine, because salvation rests on God’s promise, not on feelings. In the coming days we’ll walk with you as you see the assurance of new life and learn to grow in it. If you are still thinking it over, that’s okay too. God’s door is always open, and we are walking with you.
lessons.light: Heaven rejoices over one person because people matter more than things; one soul is more precious than the whole world. Those who are found go on to find others; those who are accompanied will one day accompany others as spiritual parents.
think: How do you feel knowing heaven rejoices over you?
If you have received Jesus, who do you most want to tell?
If you haven’t yet, what is your biggest concern right now?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for finding me as a shepherd finds his sheep, and for rejoicing over me. I want to answer your love with my whole life. Help me grow step by step in this new life. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Tell the person walking with you about your decision (or your thoughts). If you have received Jesus, try telling a family member or friend: “I believe in Jesus now.”
lessons.quick: When one person comes home, heaven throws a party.

weeks.title: Assurance of New Life
weeks.theme: Assurance of salvation rests on God’s promise, not on feelings.
group: Since receiving Jesus, what have you felt or noticed changing?
Have you ever doubted whether you were really saved?
When you stumble, how do you usually respond?
weeks.guide: New believers (former seekers) often experience doubt: “Am I really saved?” “I sinned again—does God still want me?” This week, help them build assurance on God’s word (1 John 5:11-13), not on feelings. Teach a simple way to confess (1 John 1:9), and encourage daily Bible reading and prayer. If they haven’t yet committed, this week still helps them see what those who believe in Jesus receive.
weeks.meet: This week, memorize 1 John 5:11-12 together with the person walking with you, and set the date for your next meeting.
weeks.keyText: He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life.

lessons.title: You May Know
text: The testimony is this: that God gave to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son.
He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life.
These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life, and that you may continue to believe in the name of the Son of God.
lessons.hear:
Many people say, “I hope I’ll go to heaven.” But the Bible doesn’t speak of “hoping”; it speaks of “knowing.” John says: “These things I have written to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13). God doesn’t want you to live guessing; he wants you to know for sure.

What is the basis of assurance? John says: “The testimony is this: that God gave to us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. He who has the Son has the life. He who doesn’t have God’s Son doesn’t have the life” (1 John 5:11-12). The logic is simple: eternal life is in Jesus; if you have received Jesus, you have Jesus; and if you have Jesus, you have eternal life.

It’s like a plane ticket. Whether you can board doesn’t depend on your mood today or whether you feel worthy, but on whether you hold a valid ticket. Feelings rise and fall, but God’s promise doesn’t change. When doubts come, don’t ask, “Do I feel saved?” Ask, “Have I received Jesus? What does God say?”
lessons.light: Assurance doesn’t rest on my feelings but on God’s word. The Bible is my standard: when my feelings and God’s word disagree, I choose to believe God’s word. This is the foundation for steady growth in new life.
think: Do you “hope” you are saved or “know” you are saved?
How does the plane-ticket picture help you?
When doubts come, how can you answer them with God’s word?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that I don’t only hope—I know that I have eternal life. I have received your Son Jesus, so I have life. When doubts come, help me stand on your promise. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write 1 John 5:12 on a card and keep it in your wallet or phone case. Take it out and read it when you doubt.
lessons.quick: He who has the Son has the life—a promise, not a feeling.

lessons.title: A New Creation
text: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.
lessons.hear:
Paul says: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17). This doesn’t mean all your problems disappear the moment you believe, or that every bad habit is gone overnight. It means that at the deepest level of your identity, something entirely new has happened.

Like an acorn planted in the ground: it already carries the life of an oak tree; it just needs time to grow. A newborn baby is fully human; it just needs to learn to walk and talk. Those who believe are the same: you are already a new creation, with new life, a new identity and a new direction. What comes next is that new life growing step by step into what it already is.

So when you see old habits and old tempers still in you, don’t lose heart and say, “I haven’t changed at all.” Tell yourself: “I am a new creation; these old things don’t define me anymore.” Your past doesn’t define you; your failures don’t define you. Your new identity in Christ does.
lessons.light: Changing from the old self-centered life to the new selfless life is a lifelong journey. The new life is already inside; growth is letting it be lived out. Changing life changes the way we live, and the change of life begins with a new identity.
think: Since believing (or imagining believing), which “old thing” do you most hope will pass away?
What hope does the acorn-and-oak picture give you?
What do you usually use to define yourself? What is your new identity in Christ?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for making me a new creation. I still have many old habits and weaknesses, but I know they don’t define me anymore. Let the new life in me grow day by day. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Make two columns: “The old me” on the left and “Me in Christ” on the right, with three lines each. On the right you can use the Bible’s words (loved, forgiven, a child of God).
lessons.quick: My past doesn’t define me—in Christ I am a new creation.

lessons.title: Abba, Father
text: For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba! Father!”
The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God;
lessons.hear:
Some people believe in Jesus yet remain afraid inside: afraid God is angry, afraid of being punished for not doing well, afraid of being abandoned. Paul says: “For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15).

“Abba” was the affectionate word little children used for their father—like “Daddy.” A slave trembles before his master, afraid of doing wrong; a child can come to his father to be held, to cry, to speak from the heart. God puts the Holy Spirit in the hearts of those who believe, and the Spirit lets us know from within: “I am God’s child.” Paul says: “The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God” (Romans 8:16).

This is one of the warmest parts of faith: we aren’t trying to please a harsh boss, but responding in love to a kind Father. Maybe you didn’t have a good father growing up; maybe your father hurt you deeply. The heavenly Father isn’t like that. He is the Father you have always longed for but never had. Today, try beginning your prayer with “Abba, Father.”
lessons.light: A child’s heart isn’t afraid of punishment; it trusts the Father’s love. People who are loved no longer need to prove themselves by performance—the beginning of freedom from pride and fear.
think: Is your relationship with God more like a slave and master, or a child and father?
How does calling God “Abba, Father” make you feel?
How has your experience with your own father shaped your picture of God?
lessons.speak: Abba, Father! Thank you for making me your child. I don’t have to be afraid like a slave anymore; I can tell you what’s really in my heart. Please heal the hurts in me connected with my father, and let me know your true love. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: When you pray today, begin with “Abba, Father,” and tell him one thing on your heart like a child.
lessons.quick: I am not a trembling slave—I am a beloved child.

lessons.title: When I Stumble
text: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
lessons.hear:
After believing, you may be disappointed to discover: I still sin. I lose my temper, I lie, I look at things I shouldn’t. Then a voice inside says, “You never really believed.” “God must be disappointed; he doesn’t want you anymore.” What should you do then?

John is very honest: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). Christians aren’t people who never sin; they are people who know where to go when they do. He continues: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

Confession isn’t being saved all over again; it’s like a child who broke a cup running to say “I’m sorry” to Dad. The relationship isn’t broken; it just needs mending. Confession is simple: name it specifically (not vaguely, “I’m so bad”), receive God’s forgiveness (don’t keep punishing yourself), and turn and change direction. Children learning to walk will fall. A good father doesn’t reject his child for falling; he picks the child up so they can keep walking.
lessons.light: Hiding after we stumble is pride (not wanting to admit it) or fear (afraid of punishment). Coming to confess is humility. The humble can get up after falling, because they know grace is bigger than their failure.
think: After believing (or as you imagine it), where do you stumble most often?
When you stumble, what does the voice in your heart usually say?
Are you willing to believe the promise of 1 John 1:9?
lessons.speak: Father, I confess that today (these days) I sinned against you in ___. Thank you that you are faithful and righteous and will forgive me and cleanse me. I receive your forgiveness, and I want to turn. Please lift me up so I can keep walking. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Spend three minutes before bed reviewing your day: is there anything to confess? Name it specifically, receive forgiveness, then sleep in peace.
lessons.quick: Christians aren’t people who never fall—they know where to go when they do.

lessons.title: Nothing Can Separate Us
text: For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers,
nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
lessons.hear:
Stage three is coming to an end. Over these four weeks we have seen that grace is a free gift, repentance is turning, faith is trust, receiving Jesus is letting him be Lord, and we have seen the assurance of new life. Today we close with one of the most powerful passages in the Bible.

Paul says: “For I am persuaded that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from God’s love which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:38-39). He lists everything that could frighten us—death, spiritual powers, an uncertain future—and concludes: nothing can pull us out of God’s love.

This isn’t because we hold on tightly, but because God holds on tightly. When a child crosses the street, safety doesn’t depend on how tightly the child grips Dad’s hand, but on how tightly Dad grips the child’s. In stage four we will learn to put down roots in this love: prayer, Bible reading, the presence of the Holy Spirit, facing temptation. New life needs to be well fed to grow and bear fruit.
lessons.light: Security doesn’t come from my performance but from God’s love. Only those rooted in this love have strength to deny themselves and love others. Life first, then relationships: being rooted in God’s love is the foundation of every relationship.
think: Of the things Paul lists, which do you fear most?
What comfort does the picture of a child crossing the street give you?
Looking back on stage three, how has your relationship with God changed?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you that nothing can separate me from your love—not death or life, not things present or things to come. It isn’t that I hold on to you; you hold on to me. I want to put down roots and grow in your love. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Read Romans 8:38-39 aloud, and add your greatest fear to Paul’s list.
lessons.quick: It’s not that I hold on to God—God holds on to me.
